title: Recursion and Backtracking
summary: Solve a problem by solving a smaller copy of itself, then undo choices when you need to explore alternatives.
keyPoints: Every recursive function needs a base case and a smaller recursive case.
The call stack uses O(depth) space even when you allocate nothing explicitly.
Backtracking is choose, explore, then unchoose.
Pruning skips branches that cannot produce a valid answer, often turning an impossible search into a practical one.

complexity.note: There are 2ⁿ subsets; copying them costs n each.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the base case or making the recursive input larger instead of smaller.
Mutating a shared list but forgetting to undo the change before returning.
Adding a result list directly instead of a copy, so later changes alter earlier answers.
Exploring duplicate branches without sorting or using a visited set.
interviewNotes: State the decision at each step: include or exclude, choose this candidate or skip it.
Draw the recursion tree and point out where pruning removes branches.
Always mention the depth of the call stack in the space complexity.

checkYourself.question: Why does generating all subsets take O(n * 2ⁿ) time rather than O(2ⁿ)?
checkYourself.answer: There are 2ⁿ subsets, and copying each subset into the result takes up to n work.

checkYourself.question: What does 'unchoose' mean in backtracking?
checkYourself.answer: After exploring a branch, remove the choice from the current path so the next branch starts from the same state.

checkYourself.question: How does memoization change naive recursive Fibonacci?
checkYourself.answer: Each subproblem is computed once and stored, reducing the exponential call tree to O(n) states and O(n) time.
